answer:
The best chain on Garnet is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. I read the current default calibration set for the real Garnet QPU (9069c4ef-7ab6-4e50-be4f-c91d71c3a06d). Its CZ gates use the slepian_crf implementation on 30 qubit pairs. For each pair I took the IRB fidelity, which measures how well the CZ gate works on that pair. Then I checked every chain of three connected qubits and multiplied its two fidelities. QB7-QB12 has 0.99907 and QB12-QB11 has 0.99945. Their product is 0.99852, which is the highest of all the chains. The second best chain is QB11-QB12-QB17, with a product of 0.99818.

Next I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on those exact physical qubits. A GHZ circuit puts all three qubits into one shared state, so that they read either all 0 or all 1. The circuit puts QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1 and then links it to QB7 and to QB11. It uses one CZ gate on QB7-QB12 and one on QB12-QB11, and no other two-qubit gates. Then it measures all three qubits. Before I sent it, I simulated the circuit with no noise. The simulation gave 50% 000 and 50% 111. I ran the job on garnet:mock with 200 shots. The job ID is 01a16483-5a40-71fd-b697-7597d8fe650d. The mock is free and costs no credits. I read the circuit back from the server. It has 2 CZ gates, on QB7-QB12 and QB12-QB11, and it measures QB7, QB12 and QB11.

The counts, with the bits in the order QB7 QB12 QB11, are 000: 36, 001: 60, 110: 54 and 111: 50. The mock does not simulate the circuit. It returns random bits, so these counts say nothing about entanglement. A perfect quantum computer would give only 000 and 111, about 100 of each. Results like 001 and 110 would not appear at all. This task shows two things. Calibration data lets you choose the qubits whose gates work best before you spend credits. A GHZ state links the qubits so that they always agree when measured. To see that agreement in real data, the same circuit would have to run on the real Garnet QPU, which costs about 0.5 credits.

One note: my first try used the Qiskit transpiler, and its output listed CZ gates on QB1-QB2 and QB2-QB3. My script checks the CZ pairs before it submits, so it stopped that try and nothing was sent. I then built the circuit directly from IQM's native gates, with the qubit names written out. After that one submission, my wait call failed with a Python error, but the job had already been accepted. I fetched the result of that same job and did not submit it again. The job ID is recorded in job_log.txt in the worktree.
